content: The Guideline Development Group (GDG) was responsible for organizing meetings, preparing and reviewing the final guideline document, managing feedback from external peer reviewers, and overseeing the publication and dissemination of the guidelines. Members of the WHO Steering Group, who contributed to this process, are acknowledged in the document. The WHO Guideline Steering Group selected 21 external experts, country delegates, and stakeholders from all six WHO regions to form the GDG, also referred to as the panel. This group was diverse, including professionals such as infection prevention and control (IPC) experts, clinical microbiologists, epidemiologists, public health and infectious disease specialists, researchers, and representatives from affected communities, including a patient representative. Geographic representation and gender balance were also considered in the selection process. The GDG appraised the evidence used to inform the recommendations, provided guidance on interpreting the evidence, and formulated the final recommendations. They considered the 2016 WHO guidelines on core components of IPC programs at national and acute healthcare facility levels. The GDG also reviewed and approved the final guideline document. Members of the GDG are acknowledged in the document. A Systematic Reviews Expert Group was selected by the WHO IPC Unit team, in consultation with the methodologist and GDG chair, through a bidding process. This group reviewed published evidence on the effectiveness of preventive measures during the insertion, maintenance, access, and removal of peripherally inserted catheters. They assessed the quality of evidence using the GRADE criteria specified by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. Another team of systematic reviewers, led by the methodologist, conducted a scoping review on contextual factors relevant to the priority questions addressed in the guidelines. These factors included stakeholders' perceptions of resource implications, acceptability, and feasibility of interventions to prevent bloodstream infections (BSIs) and other infections associated with the use of peripheral intravenous catheters (PIVCs) and peripherally inserted central catheters (PICCs). The findings were synthesized and presented to the GDG. The External Peer Review Group consisted of seven technical experts with extensive knowledge and experience in IPC, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), patient safety, and health management, including field implementation, as well as a patient representative. This group was geographically balanced to include perspectives from both high-income and lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). No member declared a conflict of interest. Their primary role was to review the final guideline document, identify inaccuracies or errors, and provide feedback on technical content, evidence, language clarity, contextual issues, and implementation implications. They ensured that the guideline decision-making processes incorporated the values and preferences of end-users, including healthcare professionals and policymakers. However, they were not authorized to change the recommendations formulated by the GDG. The guidelines are based on the GRADE evidence-to-decision framework, which considers desirable and undesirable effects, certainty of evidence, values, balance of effects, required resources, cost-effectiveness, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. Using this methodology, the GDG formulated conditional recommendations, which imply that most people to whom the recommendation applies would benefit from the suggested option, and in most contexts, the option can be implemented as a policy. For all conditional recommendations, the GDG provided the conditions under which the management strategy would be essential to adopt and implement for preventing PIVC-associated BSIs and related infections. The systematic reviews on the prevention of BSIs and other infections associated with PIVCs followed specific research questions in PICO format. The findings of these reviews, along with additional evidence, are included in each chapter of the guidelines and summarized in the Web Annex. All documents were shared in advance with GDG members, and the systematic review team presented the main findings. An independent methodologist facilitated discussions and the completion of evidence-to-decision tables. In addition to recommendations, the guidelines include good practice statements, which refer to practices that are widely accepted and demonstrate a clear net benefit. These statements are not formally rated for quality of evidence but are considered important by the guideline panel. The decision to develop good practice statements was discussed with the methodologist and agreed upon by the GDG. The WHO recommends that all clinicians be appropriately educated on the indications for intravascular catheter use, proper procedures for their use, and infection control measures to prevent catheter-related infections in adults, adolescents, children, and neonates. Clinicians should also be regularly assessed for their knowledge and adherence to guidelines related to managing intravascular catheters. The WHO emphasizes the importance of hand hygiene and aseptic no-touch techniques to prevent catheter-related infections. Hand hygiene should be performed according to the Five Moments during catheter insertion, maintenance, access, and removal, preferably using alcohol-based hand rubs or soap and water with single-use or clean towels for drying. Clinicians should also be trained in aseptic no-touch techniques. For the insertion of PICCs and peripherally inserted arterial catheters (PACs), the WHO recommends using a sterile technique, including sterile barrier precautions such as a medical mask, sterile gown, sterile gloves, and a sterile drape to prevent contamination. For PIVCs, an aseptic no-touch technique is considered adequate, provided there is strict adherence to all necessary steps. However, in situations where PIVC insertion is challenging, a sterile technique should be followed. The WHO also recommends adequate skin disinfection before the insertion of PIVCs, PICCs, and PACs. Chlorhexidine-containing preparations are suggested, but alternatives may be used based on local availability, context, and cost. Skin disinfectants should be allowed to dry for at least 30 seconds for maximal effect. Special considerations should be made for neonates, particularly those with a gestational age of less than 36 weeks, to avoid the risk of chemical dermatitis. The guidelines highlight the need for further research on cost-effective alternatives to sterile barrier precautions, adherence to aseptic no-touch techniques, and the use of skin disinfectants in various clinical settings. Research is also needed to better define the size of drapes required and the necessity of wearing masks during PIVC insertion.
